segments.label: macer-01-artemisia
segments.text: Artemisia — Mugwort. Macer Floridus: Among herbs artemisia is queen. It warms, expels worms, provokes menstruation, aids the traveller against fatigue. The root taken in wine drives out the stone. Applied to the navel it eases childbirth.

segments.label: macer-02-beta
segments.text: Beta — Beet. The juice of black beet dropped into the nostrils purges the head. Taken in wine it helps against serpent bite. The leaves applied warm ease headache.

segments.label: macer-03-verbena
segments.text: Verbena — Vervain. Vervain purges old fevers. Worn about the neck it heals scrofula and throat ailments. Taken with vinegar it helps the spleen and old sores.

segments.label: macer-04-salvia
segments.text: Salvia — Sage. Sage warms the sinews and drives out paralysis. The juice with wine drunk for forty days restores sensation to paralysed limbs. It sharpens memory and is good for the liver.

segments.label: macer-05-ruta
segments.text: Ruta — Rue. Rue sharpens the sight and counteracts all poisons and venoms. Mixed with honey it draws poison from the bitten. It suppresses lust when eaten frequently.

segments.label: macer-06-absinthium
segments.text: Absinthium — Wormwood. Wormwood cleanses the liver and spleen and drives worms from the belly. The juice with salt applied externally heals the mange and old sores. It repels moths from stored clothing.

segments.label: macer-07-marrubium
segments.text: Marrubium — White Horehound. Horehound with honey cooked and drunk clears the lungs and cures old coughs. The juice heals the ears. Applied with oil it removes lice from the head.

segments.label: macer-08-foeniculum
segments.text: Foeniculum — Fennel. Fennel seed and root taken in wine provoke urine and aid the kidneys. The herb promotes milk in nursing mothers. The juice sharpens dim sight when dropped into the eyes.

segments.label: macer-09-mentha
segments.text: Mentha — Mint. Mint stops vomiting and hiccough. Applied with salt it cures dog bite. Taken with honey and vinegar it dissolves congealed blood. It restrains the flow of blood.

segments.label: macer-10-urtica
segments.text: Urtica — Nettle. Nettle seed with wine and pepper provokes coition. The root with vinegar cures the mange. The boiled herb with alum stops bleeding. Taken in drink it clears mucus from the lungs.

segments.label: macer-11-agrimonia
segments.text: Agrimonia — Agrimony. Agrimony with water purges the liver. The herb boiled in wine helps wounds and heals serpent bite. It is good against tertian fever taken in wine before the fit.

segments.label: macer-12-allium
segments.text: Allium — Garlic. Garlic drunk in wine kills intestinal worms. With vinegar it cures scrofula. Cooked under embers and taken with honey it helps old coughs and clears the voice.

segments.label: macer-13-cepa
segments.text: Cepa — Onion. Onion juice with honey heals dim sight. Applied with salt and rue it draws thorns and splinters from wounds. Eaten raw it provokes sleep; the seed eaten with vinegar kills worms.

segments.label: macer-14-lactuca
segments.text: Lactuca — Lettuce. Lettuce promotes sleep and restrains carnal desire. The juice taken with vinegar helps those suffering from inflammation of the liver. It increases milk in nursing women.

segments.label: macer-15-portulaca
segments.text: Portulaca — Purslane. Purslane applied to the forehead cures headache from heat. The juice taken with vinegar and honey removes bile. It cools internal heat and quenches thirst.

segments.label: albik-01-introduction
segments.text: Medical advice of Zikmund Albík of Uničov, court physician, written for His Imperial Majesty Sigismund, Holy Roman Emperor, King of Hungary and Bohemia. On the preservation of health and the treatment of maladies afflicting persons of imperial station. Previously known from one manuscript only; this copy in MS XVII.J.28 is the second known witness.

segments.label: albik-02-regimen
segments.text: Albík on imperial health regimen: The emperor should rise at the fourth hour, take light food in the morning, avoid strong wine before midday. Exercise should be moderate — neither excessive nor absent. Rest after the midday meal is beneficial but sleep should not exceed two hours in daylight.

segments.label: albik-03-digestion
segments.text: Albík on digestion: After eating the emperor should walk one hundred paces or sit quietly. No cold water should be drunk immediately after meals. Lettuce and fennel aid digestion; onion and garlic in small amounts are beneficial to one of phlegmatic complexion.

segments.label: albik-04-fever
segments.text: Albík on fever: In tertian fever the patient should fast on the day of the paroxysm. Wormwood with wine taken before the onset of the attack gives relief. Agrimony with spring water is effective against quotidian fever. The patient should keep warm and avoid cold air.

segments.label: albik-05-wounds
segments.text: Albík on wounds in campaign: For wounds sustained in battle, apply plantain leaf bruised with salt immediately to stop bleeding. For deep wounds, pour wine into the cavity before closing. Honey mixed with white of egg draws out corruption. Wounds should be kept dry after the third day.

segments.label: czech-herbal-general-01
segments.text: MS XVII.J.28, Czech National Library, Prague. 15th century medical compendium. Contains: De viribus herbarum (Macer Floridus) in Czech translation — the only surviving Czech version of this foundational medieval plant medicine text. Also contains medical recipes, practical household remedies, and the Albík advice to Emperor Sigismund. Written in Czech and Latin, likely Bohemian provenance, c. 1400–1450 CE.

segments.label: czech-prager-wundarznei
segments.text: Prager Wundarznei (MS XVI.F.2) — Prague surgical medicine. A surgical text in the German vernacular tradition, containing treatments for wounds, fractures, skin diseases, and battlefield injuries. One of five medical manuscripts among the 31 Czech National Library manuscripts newly digitized by Manuscriptorium in 2026. Represents the practical surgical tradition of central European medicine in the 15th century.
